title: Repeat Corrosion and Skin Cracking Along the Forward Lower Fuselage Joint — Request for a Permanent Solution
abstract: Operator request for a permanent design solution to recurring corrosion and skin cracking along the forward lower fuselage joint on their oldest ZEPHYR-20 and ZEPHYR-22 aircraft, after repeated blend-outs and two engineering repairs in four years.

sections.request: Our three oldest aircraft keep coming back with the same problem on the underside of the front fuselage, just below the floor line between the two cargo compartments. We first see white powdery corrosion coming out from under the rivet heads on the overlap, and once we open it up there is nearly always a crack running from one of the fastener holes. We have blended out the corrosion four times on one aircraft and twice on two others, and the last one was too deep to blend so we had to fit a repair patch and accept an inspection every 1500 flights. Our engineers say the sealant between the two skins has simply given up after thirty years and the water is getting in from the cargo bay floor. We do not want another patch. We want a design change that we can embody in a normal heavy check and then stop worrying about this area for the rest of the aircraft's life.
sections.background: The area was first flagged by our maintenance provider during the 2022 heavy check on one aircraft and has appeared on every subsequent heavy check across the classic sub-fleet. Two aircraft now carry approved repairs with a life limit attached, and one of those repairs is already at half life. Our unscheduled findings on this zone run at 3.6 events per 1000 flight cycles against a fleet average of 0.5. We have applied the sealing improvement bulletin and the bonded strap bulletin that Aeralis offered, and the findings continued after both.
sections.expected_outcome: A permanent change to the joint itself, not another external patch, that removes the repeat inspection and that we can embody inside a scheduled heavy maintenance visit without splitting the fuselage. It must be applicable to aircraft that already carry an approved repair in the same area, and the kit must be available before our next heavy check window opens in early 2028.

type_data.business_justification: Six unscheduled findings across three aircraft since 2022 have cost an estimated 41 aircraft-days and two life-limited repairs that now drive their own inspection programme. The operator intends to keep the classic sub-fleet in service until 2034.
